Title says it all really. There are a few books I've tried to get into but just can't. The three big examples are Dracula by Bram Stoker and The Dark Tower books by Stephen King.

My problem with Dracula is the way it's written. I really like the story and mythos of Dracula but I'm not interested in reading the story through Mina and reading what she did that day. I really loved the prologue and the atmosphere created by it and then we switch to the story of an English woman talking about her day. Apparently the majority of the story is told through Mina's diary entries. I just couldn't get into it after that.

The same kind of thing happened with Dark Tower. Everything I know about the books suggest I would really enjoy them but I can't get into them. The first book is filled with a ton of lore that it doesn't try to explain. It's like you have to know everything about the books before you can even read them. Things happen with almost no explanation too. I was just left lost by the language and lack of exposition.

What about you? Have you ever ran into a book you were sure you were going to love but then couldn't get in to?

Came in here to post both Gravity's Rainbow and The Idiot. I've read other works by both authors and loved them. Can't really describe why I don't like reading GR but The Idiot just seems... too Russian for me, I guess. Maybe it's just the beginning requires a lot of formal introductions and people and little quirks of Russian high society, since it's about a guy making his debut. There were moments in The Brothers Karamazov like that (I dreaded reading the word "sensualist") but I managed to slog through them.

Underworld, The Mysterious Origins of Civilization is a book written around a fascinating concept: that civilization started thousands of years earlier than everyone thinks. The premise is that ancient civilizations were built adjacent to oceans, back when the ocean sea level was (I can't remember the exact range) 100+ feet lower than it is today. We don't see the monuments of the past because they were subsequently covered up by rising sea levels, but there are monuments right off the coasts all around the world.

It was a fascinating concept but an incredibly boring read at greater than 700 pages. The dude who wrote it was providing way, way, way too much information about how he did his research, giving a blow-by-blow account of what he did (e.g. "What next? I scrolled quickly through another article in the file....my eyes were drawn to this paragraph.") which cluttered up what his research uncovered. I made it about half-way through the book.
